title: Normalization and completion of a reduced local algebraic curve
statement: Let $k$ be a field and let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a reduced local $k$-algebra, meaning that $a^n=0$ with $n\geq1$ implies $a=0$. Assume $A$ is essentially of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-pbc-essentially-finite-type-algebra] and has Krull dimension $1$ [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Let $Q(A)$ be the localization of $A$ obtained by inverting every non-zero-divisor (an element $s$ for which $sa=0$ implies $a=0$), and let $B\subset Q(A)$ be the integral closure [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] of $A$ in $Q(A)$. Write $\widehat A=\varprojlim_n A/\mathfrak m^n$ for its completion [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion]. Tensor products mean extension of scalars [def-weil-module-base-change]. Then $B$ is a finite $A$-module [def-weil-finitely-generated-module], $\widehat A$ is reduced of dimension $1$, and the canonical map identifies $B\otimes_A\widehat A$ with the integral closure of $\widehat A$ in $Q(\widehat A)$. Here the map to $Q(\widehat A)$ extends $A\to\widehat A$ and sends the denominator of any element of $Q(A)$ to the same denominator in $\widehat A$.

source.place: Tag 0C3V (lemma-normalization-same-after-completion), completion clause, and lemma-pre-delta-invariant; specialized to local rings essentially of finite type over a field.

proof.text: First $k$ is Nagata directly from the definitions: its ideals are $0,k$, its only prime is $0$, and for every finite field extension $L/k$ the integral closure of $k$ in $L$ is all of $L$, hence a finite $k$-module. Indeed a linear dependence among the powers of an element of $L$, scaled by its nonzero leading coefficient, gives a monic equation. Write $A\cong W^{-1}T$ with $T$ a finite type $k$-algebra, and choose the defining surjection $k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\twoheadrightarrow T$. Starting from $k$, apply the polynomial-Nagata lemma $n$ times (base case $n=0$); the quotient clause of the finite-over-Nagata lemma gives that $T$ is Nagata, and the localization lemma gives that $A$ is Nagata. In particular $A$ is Noetherian. No perfection or separability assumption on $k$ is used.

Let $\mathfrak p_1,\ldots,\mathfrak p_t$ be the finitely many minimal primes of $A$. Apply the reduced-Noetherian total-fractions lemma to obtain the canonical isomorphism $Q(A)\cong\prod_i K_i$, where $K_i=A_{\mathfrak p_i}$ is a field and $\mathfrak p_iA_{\mathfrak p_i}=0$. Put $D_i=A/\mathfrak p_i$. The kernel of $A\to K_i$ is exactly $\mathfrak p_i$: one inclusion follows from the displayed vanishing, and if $a/1=0$, some $u\notin\mathfrak p_i$ has $ua=0$, so primality gives $a\in\mathfrak p_i$. Thus $D_i$ embeds in $K_i$; writing elements of $K_i$ as $a/u$ shows that it is its fraction field. Each $D_i$ is a local Noetherian Nagata domain by the quotient clause. Moreover $\dim D_i=1$: the maximal ideal of $A$ is not minimal (otherwise every prime, being contained in it, equals it and $\dim A=0$), so $\mathfrak p_i\subsetneq\mathfrak m$ gives a chain of length one in $D_i$, while any longer chain would lift to one in $A$.

source.place: Tag 0C3V, proof of the normalization/completion clause

proof.text: Let $E_i$ be the integral closure of $D_i$ in $K_i$. The Nagata condition says $D_i$ is N-2, and the Japanese-domain definition, with the degree-one extension $K_i/K_i$, says $E_i$ is a finite $D_i$-module. The one-dimensional integral-closure lemma, applied to the Noetherian domain $D_i$, gives that $E_i$ is a Dedekind domain. View $P=\prod_i E_i$ inside $\prod_iK_i=Q(A)$. Finite module generators of the $E_i$, placed in one coordinate at a time, generate $P$ over $A$, since $A\twoheadrightarrow D_i$. Thus $P$ is finite over $A$, so the finite-algebra-is-integral lemma gives $P\subseteq B$. Conversely a monic equation over $A$ for $b\in B$ projects to a monic equation over $D_i$ for its $i$th component, which therefore belongs to $E_i$. Hence $B=P$. This proves that $B$ is finite over $A$ and identifies its factors as Dedekind domains.

source.place: Tag 0C3S, finiteness of normalization; Tag 0C3V, proof; Tag 09IG for each component normalization

proof.text: For a prime $\mathfrak q$ of $B$ lying over $\mathfrak m$, the product description of $B$ selects a single factor $E_i$ and a prime $\mathfrak r$ of it: in the domain $B/\mathfrak q$, each coordinate idempotent is $0$ or $1$, exactly one is $1$, so all the other factors disappear. Consequently $B_{\mathfrak q}\cong(E_i)_{\mathfrak r}$. The contraction of $\mathfrak r$ to $D_i$ is $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak p_i\ne0$, hence $\mathfrak r\ne0$. Since $E_i$ is a one-dimensional domain, a nonzero prime is maximal: $0\subsetneq\mathfrak r\subsetneq\mathfrak r'$ would be a chain of length two. Apply the Dedekind-localization lemma to see that $B_{\mathfrak q}$ is a DVR. Its completion is a DVR by the DVR-completion lemma; the DVR definition gives its principal-ideal-domain property, and the PID-normality lemma makes it a normal domain.

source.place: Tag 0C3V, proof; Tags 00PD and 0AP1 for local normalizations and their completions

proof.text: Write $R=\widehat A$ and $C=B\otimes_A R$. Apply the finite-extension completion lemma with the Noetherian ring $A$, the finite algebra $B$, and the prime $\mathfrak m$. Since $A$ is local, $A_{\mathfrak m}=A$ (all denominators outside $\mathfrak m$ are units). It gives a finite product decomposition $C\cong\prod_{\mathfrak q\mid\mathfrak m}\widehat{B_{\mathfrak q}}$, using the tensor flip $r\otimes b\mapsto b\otimes r$. The isomorphism is compatible with both the $B$- and $R$-algebra structures. Step 4 shows every factor is a normal domain. Thus $C$ is reduced and is a finite product of normal domains.

source.place: Tag 0C3V, proof; Tag 07N9, finite-extension completion decomposition

proof.text: The Noetherian completion-flatness lemma and the definition of flatness apply to $A\to R$. Tensoring the injection $A\hookrightarrow B\subset Q(A)$ gives an injection $i:R\hookrightarrow C$, $r\mapsto1\otimes r$. Since $C$ is reduced by step 5, so is $R$: $r^n=0$ implies $i(r)^n=0$, then $i(r)=0$, then $r=0$. The completion-dimension lemma says that $R$ is Noetherian local and $\dim R=\dim A=1$. If $b_1,\ldots,b_h$ generate $B$ over $A$, the elements $b_j\otimes1$ generate $C$ over $R$, by expanding each pure tensor. Therefore $C$ is a finite $R$-module and the finite-algebra-is-integral lemma says it is integral over $R$.

source.place: Tag 0C3V, proof of the normalization/completion clause

proof.text: The finite-algebra-Noetherian lemma applies to $R\to C$, so $C$ is Noetherian and hence has finitely many minimal primes. Together with its reducedness and its finite-product-of-normal-domains description in step 5, these are all the hypotheses for the reduced-normal-total-fractions equivalence. Apply implication (3)$\Rightarrow$(2) there: $C$ is integrally closed in $Q(C)$.

source.place: Tag 0C3V, proof of the normalization/completion clause

proof.text: For the chosen finite generators write $b_j=a_j/t_j$ in $Q(A)$, where every $t_j$ is a non-zero-divisor of $A$. Put $s=\prod_jt_j$. Then $s$ is a non-zero-divisor and $sB\subseteq A$: explicitly $sb_j=a_j\prod_{\ell\ne j}t_\ell\in A$, and extend by linearity. Multiplication by $s$ on $B$ is injective because $s$ is invertible in $Q(A)$. Tensor this injection and the injection $s:A\to A$ with the flat $A$-module $R$. Thus multiplication by $s$ is injective on both $C$ and $R$. Here and below $s$ also denotes its image in these rings.

source.place: Tag 0C3V, proof of the normalization/completion clause

proof.text: The $A$-linear map $d:B\to A$, $b\mapsto sb$, induces $d_R:C\to R$, $d_R(b\otimes r)=(sb)r$. On pure tensors, $i(d_R(c))=sc$ and $d_R(i(r))=sr$, hence these identities hold for every $c,r$. Define $j:C\to R[1/s]$ by $j(c)=d_R(c)/s$. It is additive and sends $1$ to $1$. For multiplication, apply the injective map $i$ to obtain $i(d_R(c)d_R(c'))=s^2cc'=i(s\,d_R(cc'))$, so $d_R(c)d_R(c')=s\,d_R(cc')$, proving multiplicativity of $j$. If $j(c)=0$, some power of $s$ annihilates $d_R(c)$; its regularity on $R$ gives $d_R(c)=0$, hence $sc=0$ and then $c=0$. Also $j(i(r))=r$. We have therefore explicitly embedded $R\subseteq C\subseteq R[1/s]\subseteq Q(R)$.

source.place: Tag 0C3V, proof of the normalization/completion clause

proof.text: These embeddings identify $Q(C)$ with $Q(R)$. Indeed if $r\in R$ is a non-zero-divisor and $rc=0$ in $C$, multiply by $s$ to get $r(sc)=0$ in $R$, since $sC\subseteq R$. Thus $sc=0$ and $c=0$, so $r$ remains regular in $C$. Conversely if $t\in C$ is regular, then $st\in R$ is regular on $R$: $(st)r=0$ in $C$ implies $r=0$ by the regularity of $s$ and $t$ on $C$. Hence every fraction $c/t\in Q(C)$ equals $(sc)/(st)\in Q(R)$. The inclusion in the other direction sends $a/r$ to the same fraction in $Q(C)$; these formulas are inverse and agree on $C$.

source.place: Tag 0C3V, proof of the normalization/completion clause

proof.text: Under this common fraction-ring identification, step 6 makes every element of $C$ integral over $R$. Conversely, an element of $Q(R)=Q(C)$ integral over $R$ satisfies the same monic equation over $C$, so step 7 puts it in $C$. Thus $j$ identifies $C$ with the integral closure of $R$ in $Q(R)$. Finally every non-zero-divisor $t$ of $A$ remains one in $R$, by tensoring the injection $t:A\to A$ with $R$ using flatness. Thus $A\to R$ extends to $\phi:Q(A)\to Q(R)$ with $\phi(a/t)=\bar a/\bar t$. For $b=a/t\in B$, the identity $t(b\otimes1)=a\otimes1$ in $C$ forces $j(b\otimes1)=\bar a/\bar t=\phi(b)$, and $R$-linearity gives $j(b\otimes r)=r\phi(b)$. This proves that the normalization identification is precisely the canonical map with the denominator convention required in the statement.

source.place: Tag 0C3V, proof of the normalization/completion clause

proof_origin.place: Tags 0C3S and 0C3V, normalization finiteness and the finite-product-of-completed-DVRs proof; the latter argument is applied before reducedness, which then follows by the flat injection. The common-denominator computation makes the total-fraction-ring identification explicit.
